exam: A term infant at 24 h has TSB 180 µmol/L. What is the next step? — Initiate phototherapy because level exceeds the 48‑h phototherapy threshold.
How does G6PD deficiency alter management of neonatal jaundice? — Avoid oxidative drugs and monitor for rapid bilirubin rise; consider early phototherapy.
A baby presents with yellow eyes and dark urine. Which test distinguishes conjugated from unconjugated jaundice? — Direct bilirubin measurement; a high direct fraction indicates cholestasis.
What is the significance of a bilirubin rise of 10 µmol/L per hour? — Indicates rapid progression; urgent reassessment and possible exchange transfusion.
Why might a transcutaneous bilirubinometer give a falsely low reading in a dark‑skinned infant? — Skin pigmentation interferes with light absorption, under‑estimating true serum levels.
In a low‑resource setting without phototherapy units, what is an alternative management? — Intensive LED lamps or filtered sunlight exposure, ensuring eye protection and temperature control.
What red‑flag symptom should prompt immediate referral for possible kernicterus? — Lethargy or high‑pitched cry with TSB >250 µmol/L.

How does breastfeeding jaundice differ from breast‑milk jaundice? — Breastfeeding jaundice occurs early from inadequate intake; breast‑milk jaundice appears after day 4 from bilirubin‑enhancing substances in milk.
ai.title: Total Serum Bilirubin in the Neonate
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Total serum bilirubin (TSB) quantifies jaundice severity, guides treatment, and predicts risk of bilirubin‑induced neurologic damage. In low‑resource settings, clinical assessment and simple thresholds are essential.

b: Normal newborn TSB at 12 h: <85 µmol/L
Phototherapy threshold (WHO) at 48 h: 170 µmol/L for term infants
sections.p: TSB measures both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin in µmol/L. A level above age‑specific phototherapy thresholds confirms pathological jaundice.

b: Low risk: TSB <85 µmol/L at 12 h
Medium risk: TSB 85‑170 µmol/L at 12‑48 h
High risk: TSB >170 µmol/L at 12‑48 h
sections.p: Severity is staged by TSB relative to age‑specific nomograms (Bhutani).

b: Physiological breakdown of fetal RBCs (first 2‑3 days)
Breast‑milk jaundice / inadequate feeding (day 3‑7)
G6PD deficiency, sickle cell disease
Sepsis, malaria, hepatitis B, HIV‑related cholestasis
sections.p: In East Africa, the commonest causes are physiological haemolysis, breastfeeding insufficiency, and infection.

b: Unconjugated: diffuse yellow, no hepatomegaly
Conjugated: yellow plus dark urine, pale stools, hepatomegaly
sections.p: Jaundice appears as yellow discoloration of skin and sclera, often starting at the face and spreading downwards.

t.b: Is the bilirubin level above treatment threshold? – Guides need for phototherapy or exchange transfusion
Is the hyperbilirubinaemia predominantly conjugated? – Suggests cholestasis, infection, biliary atresia
Is there immune haemolysis? – Determines need for IVIG or transfusion
Is G6PD deficiency present? – Avoid oxidative drugs
Is the estimated bilirubin above the nomogram line? – Use as screening, confirm with serum when possible

b: Apnoea, lethargy, high‑pitched cry
Seizures, hypotonia
Persistent conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia >2 weeks
sections.p: Rapid rise (>8 µmol/L per hour) or TSB >250 µmol/L risks kernicterus.

b: Adequate feeding / lactation support – reduces unconjugated bilirubin
Phototherapy (blue‑light, 460‑490 nm) – converts bilirubin to water‑soluble isomers
Exchange transfusion if TSB >250 µmol/L or neuro signs – rapid removal of bilirubin
Avoid sulfonamides, certain antimalarials in G6PD deficiency
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then lower bilirubin safely.

b: Repeat TSB 6‑24 h if level is 1‑50 µmol/L below phototherapy line (per Ompath guidance)
Screen for G6PD deficiency in high‑risk families
Vaccinate against hepatitis B
sections.p: Monitor TSB every 6‑12 h until stable; educate mothers on feeding frequency.

b: Physiologic jaundice: peak <250 µmol/L, resolves by day 7
Conjugated jaundice: direct bilirubin >20 % of total
sections.p: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (cholestasis) and physiologic neonatal jaundice.

b: Rely on serum TSB when rapid rise suspected
Check for hemolysis if TSB rises >8 µmol/L per hour
sections.p: Transcutaneous bilirubin may underestimate TSB in dark‑skinned infants; hemolysis can cause rapid spikes that are missed with delayed sampling.
